Name: Elena Gold
Question: What is the current border situation between Estonia and Russia?
Answer: Last night, Russia removed the light buoys delineating the border between Russia and Estonia in the Narva river. This happened after previous reports that Russia intends to unilaterally change its maritime borders with Finland and Estonia. As Putin’s plan to “encircle Kharkiv in 2 days” miserably failed in the East of Ukraine, Russia is staging provocations right, left and centre. According to Eerik Purgel, head of the Border Guard Bureau of the Ida-Viru County, Estonia and Russia install buoys on the Narva River to mark shipping routes every spring. The buoys need to be repositioned because the riverbed changes over time, so the fairway markings are reviewed each spring. Prior to Russia's full-scale invasion into Ukraine, the buoys were installed largely by mutual agreement. However, starting in 2023, Russia has not agreed with Estonia’s position regarding the placement of buoys. This year, Russia said it disagreed with the location of about half of the planned 250 floating markers. Estonia has installed light buoys in Estonian waters based on the State Border Act and the locations of the buoys that were mutually agreed between border agencies in 2022. "We decided to install floating signs for the summer season in accordance with the agreement of 2022 because they are needed to avoid navigation errors so that our fishermen and vacationers do not accidentally enter Russian waters," Purgel explained. Estonian Prime Minister Kaja Kallas stated at the weekly press conference that this is a border incident and the exact circumstances are being clarified. Margus Tsahkna and Kaja Kallas. Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna emphasized that the incident must be approached in a calm manner, as Russia is behaving provocatively. The incident fits the pattern of Russia's behavior in recent years, Tsahkna said — other border incidents have occurred, such as airspace violations. And it’s not only Estonia that’s targeted by Russia: similar incidents occurred on Russia’s borders with Lithuania and Finland as well. As the date of the World Peace Summit in Switzerland is getting closer (the Peace Summit is scheduled for June 15–16, 2024), we can expect more provocations from Russia. They just can’t help themselves.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How do the Dutch feel about the MH17 crash?
Answer: 10 years ago, on July 17, 2014, Russian troops shot down MH17 flight over East Ukraine, killing all 298 people on board. 80 victims were kids. The flight departed from Amsterdam in the Netherlands and was headed for Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia. Nationals of 16 countries were killed in the crash: The crew were all Malaysian, while 68% of the passengers were Dutch. No wonder the Dutch and the Malaysians are the nations that feel the most aggrieved. The forces of the Moscow-based terror organization (aka the Russian Federation) looted and interrupted with the wreckage. The Donbas militants proudly posed in front of the wreckage. But despite that, Dutch investigators managed to carefully collect, transport and put together in a hangar the wreckage of the plane. After a careful analysis, they concluded that the plane was hit with the Russian “BUK” anti-aircraft missile. Immediately after the crash, Russia lied about the cause of crash by spreading dozens of false versions. This was their 1st major disinformation campaign. In November 2022, Russian citizens Igor Girkin and Sergey Dubinskiy and Ukrainian citizen Leonid Kharchenko were found guilty of 298 counts of murder and "unlawfully causing an airplane to crash" by the Court in Hague. The investigators emphasized that according to their assessment, the Buk anti-aircraft missile system, which was used to shoot down the plane, was delivered to Donbas on Vladimir Putin's order. Hundreds of hours of intercepted conversations by militants, as well as their own initial admissions that it were them who hit the plane, were heard in the court. One of such admissions was a video interview with Igor Girkin by the Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon. Gordon asked questions supplied to him by Hague investigators and it was used as evidence. (The video is published online.) Girkin, Dubinskiy and Kharchenko had been sentenced in absentia to life imprisonment. Only Igor Girkin is in prison — and he’s in prison in Russia, since July 2023, for criticizing Vladimir Putin — not for shooting down a passenger aircraft. In Russia, you have a higher chance to be labeled “an extremist” and “an enemy of the people” if you are against the war and don’t want Russians to be killing Ukrainians in Ukraine and bombing the Ukrainian cities. 2024 Russia is putting Orwell’s “1984” to shame.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why doesn't Ukraine hit Moscow every time the Soviets hit Kiev?
Answer: Yesterday, Ukrainian drones attacked targets in 5 regions of Russia, including Moscow, with Russian officials reporting that they shot down 2 drones. Radio ‘Svoboda’ found the position of the air defense systems that shot down the drone in the Kuchino district in Balashikha near Moscow. The air defense system is located at the Kuchino landfill. Using Google maps, journalist Mark Krutov compiled a map of the locations of anti-aircraft systems. He has been doing it since May 2023, when the attacks on Moscow began. If you remember, in May 2023 drones managed to hit the roof of the building inside the Kremlin wall in Moscow, targeting the Russian flag on top of it. Then, offices of Russian ministries had been attacked in the Moscow City. At one stage, the Moscow authorities sent policemen to guard the air space, whose job was to inform the ministry of defence. Then the policemen were given anti-drone guns. For weeks in 2023, Moscow airports had to halt operations for hours because of danger of drone attacks. Now, it appears that Ukraine resumed drone attacks on targets in the Moscow region. We know that Russian anti-air defence systems are the primary goals for Ukraine. If they are eliminated, it will give Ukraine the ability to hit military targets in the Moscow region. Let’s see how it goes in the next few weeks.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Why didn't Putin introduce SVO on the territory of Bryansk, Kursk, and Belgorod regions?
Answer: After the incursion of the Ukrainian troops into the Kursk region of Russia, Vladimir Putin announced “the state of emergency” in 3 border regions (Kursk, Belgorod and Bryansk) — but he didn’t include them into the “zone of SMO” (“special military operation”, as he calls Russia’s invasion of Ukraine). Instead, Putin announced the operations in the border regions a “CTO” — “counter terrorist operation”. The distinction is material: a CTO is managed by Putin’s enforcers of choice — the FSB, as opposed to the Russian army under the command of the Ministry of Defence. For instance, border patrol in Russia is also a division of the FSB. Russia doesn’t have enough forces in the Kursk region (and neither does the FSB), so Kadyrov’s commander Apti Alautdinov called on Russians to “join the final battle with the satanic forces”. (Video in the comments below.) Alautdinov’s units ran off from any fights with the Ukrainian forces on the border, where they were located, and Alautdinov explained that simply “Ukrainians walked pass them”, insisting that “nothing special had happened”. This was 3 days ago. Now Alautdinov calls on Russians to fight the Ukrainians in Kursk (under “Akhmat” brand) — Kadyrov is saving his trained forces to be able to defend his kingdom of Chechnya when Putin’s regime collapses, he has no desire to send his loyal Chechens to die for Putin. It shows that Putin doesn’t want to pull forces from Donbas, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson to fight off the incursion in the Kursk region (the logistics of moving them is also complex), and still hopes that the invasion of the Russian territory can be somehow stopped by only the forces that the FSB can find within Russia. But the desperate plea by Alautdinov demonstrates they don’t have enough forces. Interesting.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: If Ukraine conducts virtual referendums in Russian-controlled Krasnodar, Stavropol, Rostov-on-Dov, Belgorod, Voronezh, and Kursk, and if >100% of participants vote to leave Russia and to join Ukraine, then which countries will recognize the results?
Answer: Ukraine has no plans to hold any “referenda” on the territory of Russia. Fake “referenda” on occupied territories are what Russians do. All that Ukrainians want is for Russia to withdraw its troops from the territory of Ukraine and stop killing Ukrainians. Simple thing. But Putin refuses to do it.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Was Crimea always Russian?
Answer: The headline from ‘Völkischer Beobachter‘, July 4, 1942: “Crimea is German!” Hitler was excited about the capture of Sevastopol. When you want to check the ownership of a house, you go to the land titles office: it’s a registry of who is the legal owner of the land where the house is built. There is also such registry for the large pieces of land: it’s called the United Nations. This is where internationally recognized borders of the countries are recorded. If you look at this registry, it says that Crimea is Ukraine. No matter what the 21st century neo-Hitler and his newspapers claim.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How did the myth of the mighty Russian Army start?
Answer: In Nizhny Novgorod region, mobilized soldiers who were wounded are being handcuffed to a radiator in a decaying prison building. They get beaten and abused for refusing to go back to the front in Ukraine. (Video in the comments below.) Such treatment is supposed to motivate them to agree to go back to the war. At the front in Ukraine, “refuseniks” are casually shot; on the territory of Russia, they are abused and tortured by hunger, beaten, often raped. “The mighty Russian army” doesn’t exist. It never existed. There was the Soviet army, which was also built on fear, brainwashing and propaganda — but there was something else. The Soviet people who fought against Hitler troops in WWII — and prevailed, were fighting to repel the enemy and kick out the invaders from their land. This isn’t what the Russian army is doing in Ukraine — it’s not what the Russian army was doing in Georgia or Syria. No one invaded the Russian Federation since it became a country in 1991. “Every war is terrible, and the Russian-style war is ugly,” writes Mykhailo Podolyak, advisor to the office of the president of Ukraine. “Without a pity for your own and others, when destruction is preferred to capturing. The deserts scorched by Russian bombs on our land will take decades to heal. Some cities will not be rebuilt. Missile and bomb attacks on hospitals, rape of people regardless of gender and age, abduction of children, executions of prisoners and their own refuseniks – the real ‘Gerasimov Doctrine’ has turned crimes into a tactic of war,” says Podolyak. That’s the only way that the Russian army under Putin knows. They are unable to fight differently, the whole Russian army is one giant war crime. And that’s how they are trying to fight against Ukraine’s invasion in the Kursk region. “Now Putin's army is fighting on the territory of RF, shelling and storming Russian cities and towns. Russian pilots are destroying civilian infrastructure in the Kursk region with multi-kilogram bombs, forcing tens of thousands of local residents to leave their homes. Russian soldiers are looting shops and civilian homes of their neighbors,” describes Podolyak. Before, Russians were watching the war as a television show, but for hundreds of thousands of Kursk region residents, the war is now becoming close and personal. And they can feel and experience what the Ukrainian residents living near the border with Russia had been living through for years. This new reality terrifies them. As is the fact that “the mighty Russian army” can’t protect them.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What kind of drone might have been used in the attack on a Russian air base?
Answer: There is rarely a day without a Ukrainian drone attack on an airbase, a fuel depot, or an oil processing plant deep in the Russian territory. At first, Russians suspected that it were Ukrainian saboteurs that were launching drones near the strategic targets in Russia, but by now we know that Ukrainian drones can indeed fly that far into Russia. Last night, the Russians tried to transfer troops to Kursk via the Lipetsk military airfield. But things didn’t work as planned: the airfield was hit in a massive drone attack, with explosions and fires heard until the morning. Residents of Lipetsk posted videos of low-flying drones. The Lipetsk airfield is 285km from the front line. Videos show secondary detonations. Reportedly, the hits targeted ammunition storages where more than 700 guided bombs were stored. The airfield in Lipetsk housed several dozen fighter jets and helicopters. Most of them didn’t escape. The governor of the region insisted that the fire was extinguished by the morning, but photos made by locals prove otherwise. Residents of 4 nearby villages had to be evacuated. All entertainment shows in the region have been cancelled. There were also massive drone attacks last night in the Belgorod and Kursk regions. In the Kursk region, the incursion by the Ukrainian forces is ongoing. One of the most famous long-range kamikaze drones in the Ukrainian Defense Forces is the "Lyutyi" (“Fierce”). This drone is actively used for long-distance strikes on military targets. There were also Ukrainian drones sighted in Voronezh, Bryansk and Oryol regions, as well as over the territory of the occupied Crimea. According to the Russian ministry of defence, “all drones had been shot down, no losses”. The war is now firmly into the Russian territory.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What would make people laugh at Putin?
Answer: Putin’s claims about Russia’s economic “progress” are the butt of many jokes. Yesterday, at St. Petersburg’s international economic forum, Putin announced that Russia has already overtaken Japan and Germany in terms of the size of the economy, but it needs to ensure stable growth further. “Literally last week, the World Bank made additional calculations and put Russia in 4th place,” Putin announced proudly. “Russia has the fourth largest GDP in terms of purchasing power parity, as I said, ahead of Japan,” insisted Putin. I don’t know what numbers Rosstat supplies to the World Bank (the World Bank uses the official Russian statistics), but 80% of Russia looks like this: I don’t believe for a second that a Japanese worker earning the average wage can buy less food or things than someone earning the average wage in Russia. Maybe, only if they calculate how many loafs of bread one can buy (bread only), but not if you compare the actual needs of a person living a regular life. For Russians, the lifestyle of an average Japanese is the level of unaffordable luxury. Meanwhile, in the center of Moscow, on Bobrov Lane, an elevator fell out of a shaft. Just by pure luck, a person didn’t end up dead. Soon there could be many more such incidents. The Russian authorities decided to increase the service life of dilapidated lifts from 25 to 30 years. 70,000 elevators in Russia (Russia doesn’t produce lifts but had been buying them abroad all these years) are at the end of their service life. Maintenance is also an issue because of western sanctions. At the same time, the level of cajolery towards Putin is hitting record heights. At the SPIEF, the moderator of Putin’s Q&A session promoted him as a messiah whose job is “to save the world,” depicting his appointment in 1999 as an act of “God’s mercy” to Russia. Putin’s face was glowing with delight. If what Russia turned into by 2024 is an act of “God’s mercy”, I am scared to think what God’s wrath towards Russia would look like.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How might the international community respond to the events in Kursk Oblast?
Answer: Tatyana Moskalkova, Russia’s human rights ombudsman (human rights in Putin’s Russia!), called on the UN to "condemn terrorism on the part of Ukraine amid the advance of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in Kursk Oblast." Because it’s the 6th day of the Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, and no one in the world really cares. Everyone is watching Paris Olympics. Putin also invaded Crimea in 2014 during Sochi Winter Olympics. And he was going to invade Ukraine in February 2022 during Bejing Olympics — apparently, only the personal request by Chairman Xi convinced Putin to wait until the Games ended. The Ukrainian attack also coincided with the 25th anniversary of Putin in power — it was on August 9, 1999, that the first president of Russia Boris Yeltsin appointed Putin as his “successor.” Coming back to Ukraine’s incursion into the Kursk region, I’ve been waiting for calls from the known Putin’s shills to “stop the futile resistance” and “be brave enough to raise the white flag”, addressed to the Russian army. After all, in just 5 days, the Ukrainian army took more territory in the Kursk region than the Russian troops managed to capture in the whole year in Avdiivka direction. The silence with which world players reacted to Ukraine’s surprise advance into Russia is astounding. And the most indicative thing is that Putin, instead of his usual threats and nuclear blackmail, was busy signing some laws (Putin signed record 115 laws on August 8), as if this were his main occupation, calling the Kursk incursion a "situation" — the hallmark of a strong leader, no doubt. And there is much more hidden in this silence than in all the loud statements and threats that we all have heard before.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: What does Putin wish to achieve?
Answer: Despondent Putin in North Korea, silently wishing to reset the world order to October 2021, to the version of history where he never attempted to bully NATO into submission. Frankly, I think that at this point, even Vladimir Putin himself doesn’t know what he wishes to achieve — except for the magic ability to time travel and change his own actions in the past. His plan to bully NATO spectacularly backfired — and Russians are paying a huge price for it, which will be echoing through decades and generations. For starters, in just months after Putin ordered his troops to bomb Ukraine, Russia became the most sanctioned country in the world, in response to inhumane atrocities it inflicted on Ukrainians. Nothing that Putin did before had produced such results: For over 2 decades, Putin was getting more and more imperious, and the response to the atrocities he caused to peoples of neighboring countries wasn’t strong enough to stop him venturing further. Putin’s attack on Ukraine could have been successful: if in February 2022, president Zelenskyy took the Americans’ offer to evacuate, as the 65-km-long column of Russian tanks was rolling towards the Ukrainian capital and Russian paratroopers were landing at the Hostomel air field 30 km from Kyiv, then it would be “game over” for Ukraine. Instead, Zelenskyy uttered the famous phrase: “I need ammunition, not a ride.” Putin hoped to cause an “anti-Maidan coup” in Ukraine. His plan was to re-install the expired president Victor Yanukovich, who escaped to Russia in February 2014, after months of unrest in Kyiv (initially caused by Yanukovich’s reneging on his pre-election promise that Ukraine would join the EU) — and after Yanukovich helped Putin (by not acting in Ukraine’s defence) to take over Crimea. Victor Yanukovich was the 4th president of Ukraine (25 February 2010 – 22 February 2014), who infamously escaped to Russia, where he now lives. After the re-reinstatement of Yanukovich (the application for reinstatement had already been quietly filed in a Kyiv court weeks before the February 2022 invasion, so it could be processed within a day, once Kyiv was under the Russian control), a new “election” would be called, in which Putin’s relative Medvedchuk would be “elected” as the new president of Ukraine. The plan was prepared in a great detail. Putin just didn’t foresee one thing: that the Russian troops wouldn’t be able to take Kyiv. And that Zelenskyy would be able to command the support of 95% of the Ukrainian population and lead the defence (in December 2021 — 2 months before the invasion — Zelenskyy’s approval rating in Ukraine was only 30%). Putin didn’t realize how strongly Ukrainians were united against becoming a part of Russia that when he nearly reached an agreement with the Ukrainian government in March 2022, under which Ukraine would “conditionally surrender”, he decided to add “the right of veto” for Russia on what happens to Ukraine if it’s being invaded again. The agreement that Ukraine nearly signed in March 2022 — weeks into the Russian invasion — is now all but an impossible dream for Putin. He keeps returning to its conditions and crying about the spilled milk, how the bloodbath that followed “could be prevented” — if Ukraine only agreed that Russia would be forever its ruler. The infamous “Istanbul March 2022 agreements” (which had never been fully agreed on by both parties or signed) included: And to these conditions, which the Ukrainian government was considering — Putin decided to add Russia’s “right of veto” on military aid to Ukraine in case if it ever was invaded. Basically, setting Russia to face no resistance in Ukraine when the Russian troops invade again. Russia is always doing this. This has been Russia’s modus operandi since they became a state in 1991. The old USSR still had some decency on the international stage; the Russian Federation, led by the KGB-trained clique, has none. It is content with acting in the most untrustworthy and barbaric ways. After February 2022, the masks are off — and so are the gloves. Putin’s Russia stopped hiding its inhumane essence and is gleefully demonstrating its brutishness. Putin hopes that this will save him from being ousted by his own people, whom he has promised the glory of superiority over Europe and America. Meanwhile, the reality is that he has to bow to China — and even North Korea — to be able to supply his troops, which otherwise would be exterminated in Ukraine. The huge, mighty Russia is unable to even hold onto 18% of the Ukrainian territory, without being propped by a little dictatorship of North Korea. But Putin’s wish remains to rule the world. He just needs to finally take in full the Donetsk region in Ukraine — which the Russians are trying to capture for 12.5 years — and for the West to agree that he’s the perfect person to decide who is allowed to do what, on the global scale. I don’t know how about the West, but Ukrainians are certainly not going to just give Putin what is not his.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How do you interpret Putin's comment on Carlson when he said "Everyone is perpetually deceiving me."?
Answer: Poor Putin. He constantly complains about “being deceived” by the “western partners”. This year, Putin whined about being deceived by the West on January 26, February 9, March 13, 28, May 17, June 5 and 14 — that’s 7 times in 7 months. In fact, Putin is about to break his own record in whining. In the whole 2023 year, Putin complained 7 times that he had been “deceived”: on January 18, February 21, March 14, May 30, June 13, July 8, September 4. What is weird, with Putin’s dismal track record (which he admits himself), Russians still trust him to lead them to a great geopolitical victory for Russia. Go figure.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Is Zelensky a legitimate president?
Answer: Under the Ukrainian law, Volodymyr Zelensky a legitimate president of Ukraine. Under the Ukrainian law, there shouldn’t be elections while the martial law is enacted in the country. The presidential elections should be held within months after the martial law is cancelled. During the last week, Vladimir Putin, who imprisoned or killed all his political opponents (the ones who didn’t emigrate), before refusing in registration Yekaterina Duntsova and Boris Nadezhdin as candidates in 2024 Russian presidential elections (both spoke in favor of ending the war in Ukraine) — this wannabe Russian “tsar”, who changed the constitution of Russia twice, to be able to stay in power for 25 years, was using any opportunity to make a speech questioning the Ukrainian President’s legitimacy. Russian propagandists have all been given an instruction manual to do the same. Diana Panchenko, who is a former Ukrainian journalist who ran to Russia (she was even given the opportunity to interview Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko last year), launched a poll in her X account, asking whether her followers consider Volodymyr Zelensky a legitimate president of Ukraine. She got an unexpected result: Despite the huge number of bots under control of the Kremlin propaganda department, 91% of the poll participants voted “yes” in the simple 2-option poll, confirming they consider Zelensky a legitimate president of Ukraine. Over 2 days, more than 5,700 people cast their votes. Panchenko herself denies that she lives in Russia, saying that she resides in the United Arab Emirates — the destination where Putin-lovers prefer to hang out, while Moscow keeps repelling these pesky drone attacks. Despite not living in Ukraine, Panchenko keeps calling herself a “Ukrainian journalist”. Which is weird, because according to the Kremlin propaganda’s official line, “Ukraine doesn’t exist”. Putin’s propaganda is trying to stir a “discussion” about Zelensky’s “legitimacy”, but there is really nothing to talk about: Ukraine will announce presidential elections as soon as Russians withdraw their troops. If Putin wants to assist in any way, he can give an order to his commanders to bring the Russian soldiers back home. They certainly will be happy to return to their families alive.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Do you think Putin is facing a real dilemma in liberating the territory captured by Ukraine in the Kursk region?
Answer: Ukraine has captured more territory in the Kursk region in the last 2 weeks than Russian troops managed to capture in Ukraine in 8 months of 2024 – and Putin faces a real dilemma in liberating the occupied Russian land. Yesterday, Putin called a meeting on “the situation” in 3 border regions and surprised everyone by refusing to take leadership in handling the response. “As for security issues, these are problems that lie within the area of responsibility of structures of the enforcers,” Putin stated, addressing the governors of the Kursk, Belgorod and Bryansk regions, and members of the government. "I hope that … the interaction between local and regional authorities, the government, and enforcement departments has been established, and this will also play a positive role in achieving the goals that we have here," Putin added. To summarize from Putin’s doublespeak: “I’ve started the war against Ukraine, but the Ukrainian troops invading Russia — that’s not my problem… Sort it out yourselves!” Putin even had to look into his notes for the names of the 3 border regions affected by “the situation” — he read the names from his papers. At the previous government meeting on August 12, Putin demanded for the enemy to be "squeezed out" from the Russian territory. He also vouched to give a "worthy response" to Ukraine. Since then, the Ukrainian military has increased the territory under its control in the Kursk region by at least 1.5 times: on August 12, it was estimated at 800 square kilometers, and on August 20, Ukraine’s commander-in-chief said that there were already 1,263 square km under their control. After 3 bridges over the Seim River had been destroyed, another 570 square km may fall under Ukraine’s control, with 3,000 Russian soldiers at risk of encirclement. As it was happening, Putin was traveling to Azerbaijan, Chechnya, Ossetia and other Russian regions — and now he is like, “Why do you blame me?? I wasn’t even here…” Follow me for more updates!

Name: Elena Gold
Question: Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem?
Answer: A Russian deserter who was tricked to sign up for the war told ‘The Insider’ how he was nearly killed by his own Russian troops at the front, next to a pit with 20–30 bodies. He was badly wounded when his commander sent him to pick some vodka, and nearly bled out with no assistance. It was after this experience that he decided to run off. Anton (not his real name) had no intention of joining the army whatsoever. But in the fall of 2023, he went out to a shop, and a police patrol stopped him to check his documents. Anton didn’t have his ID with him and the cops took him to the police station. They put his data into a computer and told him he had an outstanding mobilization summons and would be going to the front in 3 days. They threatened that he would have huge problems for trying to skip mobilization — but there could be a way around: he could go to the enlistment office and ask to sign the contract voluntarily. The cops told him that if he signed the contract (as opposed to being mobilized), he would be able to pick an “easy” job, like helping out in a hospital. Anton came home horrified. The idea of improving his odds to get an “easy” military job as opposed to being sent to the front as mobilized seemed reasonable. He decided that if he anyway would be mobilized, he’d better become a contractor. He signed the contract on Saturday, and on Tuesday he was already sent to a unit. And — surprise, surprise! — he was sent to an assault company. A week later he was already at the front line. That was a shock for Anton: “A week ago I was sitting at home, watching videos, working, leading a normal life, and now I'm at the trenches in Ukraine.” It didn’t take long at the front for commanders to start sending people to assaults. His unit’s goal was to take a position at the edge of a village. But to get there, the soldiers had to run over 500 meters of an open space. From the Ukrainian side, that open space was controlled by a machine gun that was able to take out up to 100 people at once. The only cover a group could take was a damaged tank stranded in the middle. The commander told the assault teams to take cover and dig an outpost near the tank, to create a position from which they would be able to move further forward. Anton says it was an idiotic plan: there was no difference whether you had to run 250 or 500 meters, after 30 seconds in an open area you would be a “toast”. The commander began sending groups of 5: on the first day, 4 groups were sent, all 20 ended up dead. No one could even reach that tank. The next day another 20 people got killed. Anton says, Ukrainians have 15–20 various drones — both killer drones and reconnaissance drones — in the air at any time, day or night. The drones see any movement immediately. “It felt like the Ukrainian Armed Forces had a 50-fold advantage in drones,” he says. Then the commanders decided to send only 2 people at once. One group managed to reach the tank and dug in, and the propagandists on TV immediately began reporting that “the village was taken.” But the Russian troops still haven’t even reached it. The commander, a former security guard from a supermarket, dreamed of seeing himself on Channel 1, to feel like a hero warrior. So, he kept sending one group after the other to the slaughter, demanding that they move forward towards the village. The group that dug in near the tank managed to survive, but they needed ammunition, food, water — so, more people were sent in to deliver supplies, and they kept being shot by the Ukrainian fire. Anton says that about 70 people died there in a week, near that tank. Anton says that the worst wasn’t even the gunfire — the worst was when you leave the dugout and are completely exposed, and you realize that at any second you can be killed. “I went out to the toilet, went back 30 seconds later, and at the place where I was, 2 mortars hit” he recalls. Sometimes the Ukrainian drone operators made errors and the drones fell down, then the commanders sent Russian soldiers into the minefields to pick them up. A task from which one is unlikely to return, because no one has maps of the minefields, the mines are just thrown in, where it falls, that’s where it falls. “You have a patch of land, 4 drones fly around it. They drop something, as soon as they fly away — the next 4 are already flying. And in the distance, there are probably 5 more, coordinating fire by mortars and artillery,” explains Anton. If a drone noticed you, you aren’t allowed to hide back in a dugout — because the operator sees a glowing dot, and suddenly it disappears: it means the person has gone somewhere. Then a precise hit arrives — and minimum 5 people in the dugout will be dead. Anton says that in 2 weeks, only 15–20 people were left from 250 soldiers that arrived, and from them 10 people were the commanders and non-combat clerks. Most of the soldiers were contractors, only a few were “mobilized”. From the losses, about 40% are dead, the rest are wounded. About 50% of the wounded are without legs or arms — disabled for life. “When I arrived, that village was still more or less intact. 3 weeks later it was just ruins. Heaps of corpses…” recalls Anton. He survived because he was part of the “evacuation team” — and he refused to go in the assaults, saying he would continue performing the task he was assigned to do. He was still going to the position near the tank, but his job was to pull the wounded, not carry provisions or stay in the dugout. Although Anton didn’t do any specific medical training, he had to perform an amputation in the field. This was like a horror movie. He pulled a guy who was lying wounded in the field for 3 days. The guy managed to apply tourniquets to wounds on his arm and leg, but after these 3 days his arm began to rot. The medics told him on the radio he had to amputate the arm. Anton injected the guy with all sedatives he could find and chopped the arm with an axe. It took him 4 attempts to get through the flesh and bones, then he had to treat the stump and bandage it. “I didn't sleep for two days after that,” Anton says. “When we were loading him [for evacuation], he was still alive, and he also made it to the first line alive. I don't know what happened to him after that.” Another guy that Anton pulled out had part of his jaw torn off, his arm up to the shoulder and half a leg. Question: Whatever happened to Mathias Rust the German man who landed a plane in Moscow during the 1980s?
Answer: 37 years ago, on May 28, 1987, German man Matthias Rust's plane landed on the Red Square in Moscow. 19-year-old German teenager initially intended to land in the Kremlin, but he decided that landing inside, hidden by the Kremlin walls, would have allowed the KGB to arrest him and deny the incident. This is why he changed his landing place to the Red Square. Rust flew his Reims Cessna 172P from Helsinki, Finland, which was the last stop of his long trip. He designed the trip purposefully, to avoid flying over the East Germany’s air space. Instead of returning to Hamburg, as authorized, he flew to Moscow. On the approach to Moscow, there was a major concentration of fighter bases and the air space was very busy. Radars and surface to air missile sites were supposed to be on alert against any enemy threats. Rust evaded it all by flying his Cessna at roof-top height, and managed to land on stone-paved Red Square, near the famous cathedral. His passing so deep into the heart of the USSR and landing in the most iconic square of Moscow, caused an immense humiliation to the Soviet War Machine — although the KGB tried to play it down. Rust managed to show just how rusty the Soviet defence really was. In fact, the whole Soviet Union was rusty. Rust was prosecuted in the USSR for entering the Soviet air space without authorization and “malicious hooligansim”, and sentenced to 4 years in a labor camp — of which he only served 14 months. In August 1988, Rust was pardoned and released, and he returned to Germany. This was in the middle of Perestroika, announced by Mikhail Gorbachev in April 1987 — weeks before Rust’s scandalous arrival. Then things went wrong for Rust, until they got better. Within a year of returning to Hamburg, he stabbed a colleague at a hospital where he worked (a female nurse who refused his advances), and ended up for 15 months behind bars again. Blame the Russian prisons for his disturbed mental state. When freed, he became a financial analyst and a yoga instructor. Reportedly, he also played high stakes poker, which he used as an income stream. Mathias Rust in 2012. He doesn’t give comments to media anymore. Rust stated he had no regrets about what he did. He was happy that he was able to help President Gorbachev to initiate his reforms. Rust's flight through the extensive Soviet air defence system — presumed impenetrable — indeed helped Mikhail Gorbachev in the implementation of his reforms. Gorbachev was able to dismiss numerous military officials opposed to his policies. Among them, the Minister of Defence Sergei Sokolov and the Commander-in-Chief of the Air Defence Forces Alexander Koldunov were fired. Over the next few months more than 150 people lost their jobs. Soviets returned Rust’s Cessna to his flying club. It changed hands a few times, until it finally found its place in the Deutsches Technikmuseum in Berlin, as a symbol of one audacious pilot’s attempt to improve relations between East and West.

Meanwhile, residents of Russian town of Belgorod seem to be waking up from the propaganda-induced dream. “Why do we live like this? Why there’s no protection for people? Why don’t we have bomb shelters? Why are we forced to hide in basements? Why are we forced to evacuate somewhere – we don’t even know where, to leave our apartments? Why do they adopt laws about mass burials in peaceful time? What does it mean? What do these laws involve?” asked the delegate from the group that united representatives from several border regions. Belgorod region is under daily strikes from Ukraine, which are targeting military facilities and artillery locations that attack Kharkiv region of Ukraine since February 2022. Belgorod residents don’t want to evacuate because their homes will surely be looted and most likely also destroyed: if people are gone, Russian troops use their homes as fortifications. The speaker continued: “We will demand that those responsible for protecting the population are held accountable. We demand an immediate resignation of the president of the Russian Federation, Putin Vladimir Vladimirovich.” The activists also demanded the governor of Belgorod region to resign and be checked for the crimes of negligence and sabotage. This is very different to regular video appeals that Russians record (usually standing on their knees) begging Putin for help. There were power outages in Belgorod region lately, so the people weren’t getting their regular daily dose of TV propaganda. Maybe that’s the reason why their eyes suddenly opened to the true reasons for their misery?

Question: What should Ukraine do in response to Putin's ceasefire conditions?
Answer: TAP ON THE PHOTO TO VIEW. I think Ukraine should put forward a counter offer to Putin: 1.Russia is leaving the territory of Ukraine, up to the internationally recognized 1991 borders. Whether Russian troops leave on their own or in black plastic bags, that’s up to their commanders. Ukraine will accept either option. 2.Putin, all the generals and top propagandists board a plane and fly to The Hague. The plane should be piloted by fighter pilots who bombed Mariupol and Kharkiv. The plane should be loaded with sufficient quantities of hand grenades and all the passengers are required to juggle grenades while in the air, Prigozhin-style. If their juggling skills are sufficient and God is with them (as they claim), they will land safely and will face the International Criminal Court. 3.In Russia, a provisional government will be appointed for the time of temporary occupation. The provisional government will be operating until everything that was destroyed in Ukraine is restored and the last hryvnia of compensation is paid to the families of those killed or misplaced by the Russian aggression. 4.Any region of the Russian Federation can secede and become independent. The regions also can unite with anyone they want, whenever they want and speak whatever language they want. The separated former constituent entities of the Russian Federation will receive a 20% discount on payment of reparations. 5. Russia’s nuclear weapons (if there are any) and all military aviation must be surrendered. That’s an absolute precondition of ceasefire. 6.The Minsk dictator’s death sentence execution should be televised to those who are unable to attend. Since Belarus have cancelled the moratorium on death sentences, and the number of victims of Lukashenko’s regime is in millions, such a measure seems appropriate. I think I have covered the most important bases, but feel free to add your suggestions in the comments below!

Question: What do Czech people think of Russians?
Answer: The Russian embassy in Prague got a makeover. In March 2022, the name of the street where the Russian embassy is located in the Czech capital was changed to “Ukrainian Heroes”. So, the address of the Russian embassy in Prague now: 6 Ukrainian Heroes Street. Czechs want Russians to know what they think about their genocidal war in Ukraine.

Question: Is peace with Putin possible?
Answer: Yesterday, all media reposted Reuters article, saying that Putin wants to freeze the war in Ukraine — citing “4 Russian sources” with knowledge of what’s happening in the top power circles in Russia. Question: What do you think are the "traditional family values" that Russia, as touted by President Vladimir Putin, has?
Answer: Russia’s top promoter of “traditional values”, 39-year-old Maria-Lvova-Belova — children’s ombudsman and mother of 10 kids, including 5 adopted kids (she’s indicted with Putin for stealing Ukrainian kids by the Hague court) — just left her 42-year-old priest husband Pavel Kogelman and moved to live “in sin” with 50-year-old oligarch Konstantin Malofeev. In another “happy family” of Putin’s supporters, entrepreneur Tatyana Bakalchuk, founder of ‘Wildberries’ — an online shopping platform a-la Amazon, which controls 5% of the online retail sales in Russia, sought a protection of Vladimir Putin himself, to avoid paying 50% in divorce to her husband. Then suddenly, Chechen leader and Putin’s close associate Ramzan Kadyrov uploaded a video, where Tatyana’s husband Vladislav asks Kadyrov for help, claiming his wife and business were highjacked from him. Kadyrov says it looks like an illegal raid and promises to help, to “go to the end.” He also promises “to return the wife home.” Tatyana responded with her own video: "This is not a corporate raid. From the very beginning, everything was agreed upon with Vladislav, he was personally present at the presentation to the top management of the new structure of the merged company.” Oligarch Kerimov also responded to Kadyrov’s threats: "He [Kadyrov] needs to get permission from Putin to talk to me. And he won't get it.” What is going on? The Bakalchuks had been divorcing for some time. In the process, they began dividing the business. It became too complex, and Tatyana went to Kerimov for support and his people designed the “merger” deal. Vladislav obviously didn’t realize at first what was happening, but when things began moving, he figured out that there soon would be nothing left in the business to divide, and contacted Kadyrov with the help of a mutual friend. There is also the curator of the deal from the presidential administration, Maxim Oreshkin. In June, Putin was brought a piece of paper asking him to bless the "merger" of ‘Wildberries’ with ‘Russ Outdoor.’ The paper said that as a result, an alternative to the evil Western SWIFT system would be created, rubles would be accepted all over the world, Russia's "soft power" would expand, and promised many other gargantuan schemes that the "great geopolitician" is so fond of. Of course, Putin got excited and gave the order to support the project. As it turned out, Kadyrov himself wanted to get ‘Wildberries’ and is now outraged. The main issue here: the merger is in favor of Suleiman Kerimov, a Dagestani. And Kadyrov, a Chechen, is an enemy of the Dagestani clan. In mafia states, mafias compete with each other. Kadyrov cannot be unaware that Putin personally blessed the merger. However, he publicly interferes. And promises to "deal with the people from the Caucasus" (hinting at Kerimov). The spiders in the jar are devouring each other ever more eagerly. As the feeding grounds shrink because of the western sanctions and the need to spend funds on the war in Ukraine, private businesses keep being seized and plundered by Putin's henchmen. That is why Russian entrepreneurs preferred to do business in Western jurisdictions. So that disputes could be resolved in a London court, and not through Ramzan Kadyrov. Russia is a hypocritical mafia state trying to mask its crimes against humanity as the drive for “traditional family values”. But at the top, it’s full of filth and moral decay. Putin himself hides his wife and kids and even the fact of their existence — it’s known that Putin has 5 or 6 kids from 3 women, and he only married and divorced one of them — his first wife Liudmila. He had been cheating on her with his current de facto partner and wife of 2 (or 3) of his kids Alina Kabaeva, whom he met when she was just a teen. Kabaeva’s lover, singer Murat Nasyrov, fell out of a window in 2007. These Russian windows are very dangerous! Apparently, the secret affair between Vladimir Putin and Alina Kabaeva began in 2006. A few months later, Kabaeva accidentally said to trusted friends that she still loved Nasyrov, with whom she had an affair in early 2000s, and he was the best man she ever was with. Then Nasyrov accidentally fell out if a window. Nasyrov and Kabaeva. Another proponent of traditional values, Ramzan Kadyrov, has 6 kids with 3 other women, in addition to the several kids with his first wife Medni, to whom he’s still officially married (and the Russian laws only allow a man to have 1 wife). To the public, the kids from the other 3 women are presented as the children of his first wife Medni. But everybody knows it’s not true, and Kadyrov himself isn’t hiding it either, by showcasing all of his kids on group family photos. These young women who became mothers of his kids were only 14 and 15 when Kadyrov “took them as wives.” There are also numerous young women in Chechnya whom Kadyrov took as concubines. These women now cannot get married. These are the “traditional values” that the rulers of Russia live in their own lives. The state of filth in the top levels of the Russian society is sickening. So is their hypocrisy.

Question: Why is Viktor Yanukovych (former President of Ukraine) meeting with Lukashenko in Belarus today (24 May 2024)?

Name: Elena Gold
Question: When will Putin stop?
Answer: If Putin were locked in a prison cell, this madness of a full-scale war in Ukraine and constant Russian threats would certainly stop. Failing that (which would be only possible through an internal coup), Putin would be forced to stop if he could no longer draft enough soldiers to send to the war in Ukraine or was unable to equip them with weapons. Willingly, Putin might stop if he were given an appearance of a victory in Ukraine: something that he could announce to the Russian populace as a triumph. For 2.5 years of the full-scale war, the Russian populace had been diligently suppressed to the level where they don’t dare to speak up — they can’t even verbalize their dismay with being “best friends” with the North Korea, which for decades has been the butt of every joke about backward dictatorships. The Russian people have to swallow their nationalistic chauvinism and display satisfaction about “strategic alliance” of Putin and Kim Jong Un. Despite numerous failures in Ukraine, Putin’s propaganda still claims that Putin is “winning” — and that they “haven’t really started yet”, and the Russian population accepts it as the indisputable truth. So, whatever Putin decides to announce as a “victory” in Ukraine, wouldn’t be disputed by the population — no matter how shameful the conditions of the deal would be for Russia. Putin’s refusal to give up isn’t because of him being afraid to lose power — it’s purely an obsession. Putin made a mistake and refuses to admit it, pretending “all is going according to plan”. Alas, the likelihood of Putin’s getting to his senses and starting to make decisions that are rational (i.e. good for Russia and Russians) isn’t high. Most likely, he would do anything to continue the war in Ukraine, hoping he’d have a chance to prevail if his army were able to last another few months — ad nauseam. Meanwhile, Russia’s economy is in deep trouble, which even the Russian officials can no longer deny. In words of the first deputy chairman of the Central Bank Vladimir Chistyukhin, the system is on the brink of a “collapse”, because of Russia’s incorrigible dependency on import. In other words, if Russia can’t import goods and services, its economy would crash within months. The latest western sanctions severely impacted Russia’s ability to pay for imported goods via legitimate payment methods, and the Russian Central Bank is unable to bypass this block, desperately researching crutch options, including barter and use of cryptocurrencies. Putin is willing to bet Russia’s present and future on his neo-USSR project. And he is convinced that Ukraine is ‘the Holy Grail’ that would tip the scales in his favor. But for that, he needs the whole of Ukraine — he can’t allow any part of Ukraine, especially Kyiv, to stay out of his grasp. He needs Odesa, he needs Mykolaiv, he needs Kharkiv. He can’t get it by force — not for the lack of trying. Putin is prepared to try to get it by other means, and his preference would be to turn Ukrainians against their government, to instigate an “anti-Maidan” coup, and install a puppet government to rule over Ukraine. That in his view is the most promising and cost effective course of action, and that’s why anyone in the west willing to sell out to Russia gets paid handsomely — Jason Hinkle recently bragged he bought a plane from his earnings on X-Twitter: Kremlin bots promote threads through incessant commenting and reposts, and Musk pays out the cash. Simple scheme. Just remember: Putin’s goal is the destroy the USA, EU and NATO. Even if the war in Ukraine stops, Putin won’t stop the war against the West. Only a change of regime in Russia can stop it.

Name: Elena Gold
Question: How are Ukrainians coping with the constant bombardments in their cities?
Answer: “I'm fine :)” installation made of Ukrainian road signs riddled with shrapnel and bullet holes at the "Burning Man" festival in the Black Rock Desert in Nevada is such a perfect expression of how Ukrainians feel. (Video in the comments below.) Usually people in Ukraine answer "Fine" to the question "How are you?" But every Ukrainian had lost friends, family members, neighbors or colleagues to this war. Every Ukrainian personally knows someone who is now at the front line, defending the country with weapons in his or her hands. 2 heroes. At the 2024 Paris Paralympics, Ukraine has the largest delegation in its history. You don’t need to guess why. The residents of small Ukrainian towns and villages located near the border with Russia are hit the hardest. They went to bed at home, and in the morning they lost everything — lucky to have survived at all. For 2.5 years, Ukrainians don’t let Russia to break their spirits. When Ukrainians answer, 'I'm fine', they mean that they continue being resilient, continue staying strong, continue choosing to be fine. Class of 2022 graduate in her prom dress on the rubble of her Kharkiv school, destroyed by the Russian artillery. “Each Ukrainian living now is a winner. The one whose family survived and got through the horrible past of occupations, genocides and wars,” writes Anton Geraschenko, former advisor to the minister of internal affairs of Ukraine. “We know what it's like to fight for our existence. We know what it’s like to protect our land. We fight and we stand now. We know how to survive, and now we will win this battle,” asserts Gerashchenko. Yana Zalevskai is a 23-year-old soldier of the 59th Brigade. She was 13 in 2014, when Russia invaded Crimea and Donbas. Yana is from Kherson. During the Russian occupation of the city in 2022, she attended anti-Russian rallies. After the city was de-occupied by the Ukrainian army, she decided to join the defenders — first as a combat medic, and then she learned to be a drone operator. Yana's father is also a soldier and has been fighting Russians in Donbas since 2014. Yana’s mother and daughter are waiting for her return at home. Yana was injured in early August and is now recovering. "I really want to end this war. I don't want our children to go to war,” says Yana. Ukrainians are resilient because they have to outlast Russia in this war. Because otherwise, there will be no Ukraine. Because they don’t want to leave this war to their kids. War and genocide must become something not to live through, but a thing from history books. The Ukrainian children should be able to grow up in peace and safety. That’s what drives Ukrainians to keep going, no matter what.
